loveday_forster_usage: colour — simple colours belong to the four elements; intermediate colours arise from mixture and blending; the central object of the treatise.
notes: No distinction drawn between chrōma and chroia as in Sens. The De Coloribus colour theory lacks the concept of to diaphanes entirely.

loveday_forster_usage: mixture, blending — the primary mechanism for generating intermediate colours from simple ones; covers physical mixing and observational chromatic variation.
notes: Less technically precise than the mixis of Sens. ch. 3, which distinguishes mixture from juxtaposition and superposition.

loveday_forster_usage: light is the colour of fire; darkness is privation of light, not a colour; the interaction of light and darkness with the four elements generates simple colours.
notes: Darkness explicitly distinguished from black: darkness has no definite magnitude or shape, but black is a genuine colour of transmuted elements.

loveday_forster_usage: maturation — the natural process by which heat, nutriment, and moisture drive chromatic change in plants and animals; fruit progresses from herb-green through a chromatic sequence; the central explanatory principle for chs. 5-6.
notes: The term πέψις is not explicitly used in the text but the concept of heat-driven concoction governs the entire biological colour theory of chs. 5-6. Presupposes Meteorology IV.

loveday_forster_usage: elements (fire, air, water, earth) — the four elements to which simple colours belong; the material substrate of all colour generation.
notes: The element-colour mapping: white to all four by nature, yellow to fire/sun, black to elements in transmutation.

loveday_forster_usage: nutriment — determines animal colouring through moisture cycles; white when moisture dries, black when it settles and becomes stale.
notes: The nutriment theory of animal colour extends the plant-maturation framework of ch. 5 to the animal kingdom in ch. 6.

loveday_forster_usage: dyeing — the paradigm case of colour transference through moisture and heat entering pores; sources include flowers, plants, roots, bark, animal juices (purple-fish), wine, smoke.
notes: Used as analogy throughout: as dyed material takes colour from dye, so fruit takes colour from juice during maturation.

loveday_forster_usage: lustre — continuity and density of light; a property of light rather than colour; explains glistening gold, pigeons' necks, falling water.
notes: Distinguished from colour proper; lustre is a light-phenomenon, not a chromatic quality.

loveday_forster_usage: black/white — the extreme colours from which all intermediates arise by mixture; white is natural colour of elements and colour of deviation/weakness; black is colour of transmutation.
notes: In the biological sections (chs. 5-6), white = weakness/ageing/deviation; black = nutriment settling and becoming stale.
